anchors.fact: Angostura began in the 1820s as a stomach medicine, made by a surgeon serving with Bolívar's forces in Venezuela, and sold abroad as a remedy. It found its way into drinks "off-label", and most recipes that call for it still use a few dashes. Only gentian and "other spices" are on record: the recipe is secret.
anchors.meaning: A thing used for what it was never meant for, and used well. That's this person with everything they touch. Say "warm spice", never "cinnamon" or "clove".
anchors.speaksTo: lens: One of my many selves · drawnToward: Change · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: In Brooklyn, Giuseppe Gonzalez made a sour with an ounce and a half of Angostura as its base and only half an ounce of rye.
anchors.meaning: Asking what happens with an ounce of what everyone uses by the dash. It's finding out, not defying anyone. No year (sources give 2008 and 2009), and never "he took it from" anyone.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Wonder · soughtFor: A little chaos

anchors.fact: By his own telling, it didn't win the competition he made it for, he was told nobody would drink it, and he kept making it.
anchors.meaning: Failure barely touches them. Always signposted ("he says", "the way he tells it"). The menu reprint stays out: it's disputed, and it reads as rule-breaking.

anchors.fact: It wasn't an immediate hit. It spread onto menus and spawned many variations, and the *Oxford Companion* uses it as its example of a drink that looks absurd on paper and works in the glass.
anchors.meaning: It didn't stop at one recipe. Other people made their own versions, which is how this person would want their work treated. Never "never settled".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Freedom · lens: My inner child

anchors.fact: In the printed recipe the whiskey is the small part, half an ounce. Here that slot is the guest's: any unsweetened spirit. The *Cocktail Codex* says a swapped spirit keeps a sour balanced but can't promise it'll taste good.
anchors.meaning: Never the same drink twice. The recipe is ours (lemongrass replaces his orgeat): keep his ounce and a half, never "his recipe". "Balances", not "works".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Change · soughtFor: A little chaos · texture: Excited

cocktail.closingLine: It'll balance whichever spirit you pour. Whether you like it is the experiment.
method: Put a coupe in the freezer.
Pour the Angostura, the lemon juice and the lemongrass syrup into a shaker. Yes, all 45 ml of the bitters.

Now pick the accent: any unsweetened spirit on your shelf, such as rye, gin, mezcal, rum, brandy or whisky. Not a liqueur; it would make the drink too sweet. Try one you haven't used here before. Add 15 ml.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain it into the cold glass.
cocktail.name: Off-Label

preparations.text: (makes about 250 ml; keeps two weeks in the fridge): slice 2 lemongrass stalks thinly and bruise them with the back of a knife. Warm them in a pan with 200 g sugar and 200 ml water, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Take it off the heat, leave it for 30 minutes, then strain it into a clean bottle.
preparations.title: Lemongrass syrup

recipe.item: Angostura aromatic bitters (recommended; or another aromatic bitters)
the accent: any unsweetened spirit you have open (rye, gin, mezcal, rum, brandy, whisky)

cocktail.tagline: You've never made the same thing twice. Not even when you tried.

reading.epigraph: Bitters usually come by the dash. This drink is built on them.
whoYouAre: Hand you instructions and you'll follow them, right up to the moment you don't. You start things before you know what they'll be. That isn't a hole in the plan. It's the part you like best: finding out.

Some of what you try doesn't work, and you honestly don't mind. You rarely mention those ones, and there are more of them than anyone guesses. What gets under your skin is the opposite: something works, and everyone wants it exactly like last time. Being asked to repeat yourself feels like a door closing. Stand next to you long enough and people start saying what you say: "let me try something." You've shown them that something that didn't work isn't a disaster. It's just the next thing to change.
yours: You've probably seen the bottle behind a bar. Almost nobody pours more than a few dashes of it. It's Angostura, and it began in the 1820s as a medicine: a surgeon in Venezuela made it for soldiers' stomachs. It was never meant for drinks. Bartenders borrowed it anyway, and in their hands it stayed a seasoning, hardly ever the main thing.

Then a bartender in Brooklyn, Giuseppe Gonzalez, made a sour (spirit, citrus and sugar, shaken) with an ounce and a half of it. The bitters became the base. The whiskey, just half an ounce, became the accent. The way he tells it, the drink didn't win the competition he made it for, and he was told nobody would drink it. It wasn't an immediate hit. But it spread, and the *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* now uses it as its example of a recipe that looks absurd on paper and works in the glass.

He wasn't trying to be clever, I like to think. He just wanted to know what would happen. That's the question you ask about everything, and like him, you'd rather find out than be told. And it didn't stop at one recipe. Bartenders went on to make their own versions of it, which is exactly how you'd want something of yours to be treated.

So the cocktail I've made for you keeps his ounce and a half of bitters and his lemon, and changes two things. His almond syrup is gone. In its place is a syrup of lemongrass, which sits beautifully beside warm spice and citrus. And his half ounce of whiskey is now yours to choose: any unsweetened spirit you have open. Gin, mezcal, rum, a smoky whisky. Every one balances, and every one makes a different drink. It's shaken hard and served in a wide, shallow stemmed glass. The bitters stay. Only the accent moves.

It didn't win, Gonzalez says, and he kept making it anyway. Somewhere you've got something you left half-tried: a recipe, a plan, an idea you walked away from just as it started working. Go back to it. Not to make it the way it was. To find out what it turns into when you stay.
